content: The recommendations for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) remain unchanged. A treatment regimen lasting 6–9 months, consisting of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), may be used under operational research conditions for MDR-TB patients with tuberculosis resistant to fluoroquinolones. This is applicable to patients who have not been previously exposed to bedaquiline and linezolid or have been exposed for no more than two weeks. The World Health Organization (WHO) also suggests a 6-month regimen of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid (600 mg), and moxifloxacin (BPaLM) for MDR/RR-TB patients, rather than longer regimens of 9 or 18 months. For MDR/RR-TB patients who have not been treated with second-line medicines for more than one month or in whom resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents has been excluded, a shorter all-oral regimen lasting 9–12 months is recommended. This regimen should include bedaquiline, provided the patient meets eligibility criteria. If only one or two Group A agents are used, both Group B agents must be included. If necessary, Group C agents may be added to complete the regimen. Kanamycin and capreomycin should not be included in the treatment of MDR/RR-TB patients on longer regimens. Levofloxacin or moxifloxacin should be included in longer MDR/RR-TB regimens, as they are strongly recommended with moderate certainty of evidence. Bedaquiline is recommended for patients aged 18 years or older on longer MDR-TB regimens and may also be included for patients aged 6–17 years. For children under 6 years with MDR/RR-TB, an all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline may be used. Linezolid is strongly recommended for inclusion in longer MDR/RR-TB regimens. Clofazimine and cycloserine (or terizidone) may also be included, but this is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. Ethambutol and pyrazinamide may be included in longer regimens, but their inclusion is also conditional with very low certainty of evidence. Delamanid may be included in the treatment of MDR/RR-TB patients aged 3 years or older on longer regimens. For children under 3 years, delamanid may be used as part of longer regimens. Imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem may be included in longer regimens, but only when administered with clavulanic acid, which is available in combination with amoxicillin. However, clavulanic acid is not counted as an additional effective TB agent and should not be used without imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem. Amikacin may be included in the treatment of MDR/RR-TB patients aged 18 years or older on longer regimens if susceptibility is demonstrated and adverse reactions can be adequately monitored. If amikacin is unavailable, streptomycin may replace it under the same conditions. Ethionamide or prothionamide may only be included in longer regimens if bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, or delamanid are not used, or if better options are unavailable. For MDR/RR-TB patients on longer regimens, a total treatment duration of 18–20 months is suggested for most patients, with modifications based on the patient’s response to therapy. If amikacin or streptomycin is included, an intensive phase of 6–7 months is suggested. For patients with rifampicin-susceptible and isoniazid-resistant tuberculosis, a 6-month regimen of rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin is recommended. Streptomycin or other injectable agents should not be added to this regimen. Monitoring of MDR/RR-TB treatment should include sputum culture in addition to sputum smear microscopy to assess treatment response. Monthly sputum cultures are desirable. Antiretroviral therapy is recommended for all patients with HIV and drug-resistant TB requiring second-line antituberculosis drugs, regardless of CD4 cell count, and should be initiated as early as possible (within the first 8 weeks) after starting antituberculosis treatment. Elective partial lung resection (lobectomy or wedge resection) may be considered for patients with rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB alongside a recommended MDR-TB regimen. Care and support for MDR/RR-TB patients are addressed in a separate sub-module of the WHO consolidated guidelines.
